article.title: The Economics of Queueing: Why Utilization Near 100% Creates Delays
article.why: Connects operations economics, utilization, waiting time, resilience, and invisible work-in-process.
article.author: OpenAI learning editor

paragraphs.en:
Organizations often try to maximize utilization. A call center wants agents busy, a factory wants machines running, a hospital wants expensive equipment used, and a cloud team wants servers efficiently loaded. Low utilization can look like waste. Yet systems that operate close to 100 percent utilization often experience rapidly growing delays.

The reason comes from queueing. Work does not arrive at perfectly regular intervals, and service time is not perfectly constant. Some customer calls take two minutes and others take twenty. Some software jobs finish quickly while others encounter complex data. Even if average capacity is slightly higher than average demand, random variation creates moments when more work arrives than the system can immediately process.

When spare capacity is available, the queue can shrink after a busy period. When utilization is extremely high, there is little spare capacity to absorb that variation. New work waits behind existing work, and the backlog can grow faster than managers expect.

A simple example shows the intuition. Imagine a team that can handle an average of 100 cases per day and receives 90. At 90 percent average utilization, there is some room to recover after a difficult morning. If demand rises to 99 cases, the system appears only nine percentage points busier, but its recovery capacity has fallen from ten cases to one. A small shock can now create a queue that takes many days to clear.

This is why waiting time often increases nonlinearly as utilization approaches the limit. The relationship is not a simple straight line. A few extra percentage points of utilization near full capacity can produce a disproportionate increase in delay.

The lesson matters for staffing. A manager may see employees with occasional idle minutes and conclude that headcount should be reduced. If those idle periods are the buffer that absorbs demand variation, removing them can increase customer waiting time dramatically. The cost saving from higher utilization must be compared with the cost of delay, abandonment, overtime, and employee stress.

The same logic applies to project teams. If every specialist is scheduled at 100 percent, any unexpected issue causes downstream tasks to wait. People begin multitasking, priorities change frequently, and coordination overhead rises. A team can be individually busy while the overall system becomes slower.

Queueing also changes how managers should interpret backlog. A growing queue is not always evidence of higher demand or poor employee effort. It can be a mathematical consequence of operating too close to capacity under variable arrivals and service times.

There are several ways to improve the system. One is to add capacity. Another is to reduce variability by standardizing common work, separating simple and complex cases, or scheduling predictable tasks. A third is to shape demand, for example by appointments, pricing, or incentives that move activity away from peak periods.

Pooling can help as well. If several small teams each maintain separate capacity, one team may be overloaded while another is idle. A shared queue can allow available capacity to serve the next task, although specialization and priority rules may limit how much pooling is practical.

Managers should also distinguish utilization targets by service requirement. A batch-processing system that can wait overnight may tolerate very high utilization. An emergency service that must respond immediately needs much more reserve capacity. There is no universal ‘good’ utilization rate.

Measurement should therefore include both efficiency and flow. Track utilization, queue length, waiting time, abandonment, throughput, and variability together. Optimizing only one can damage the others.

The economic trade-off is between the cost of spare capacity and the cost of waiting. Spare capacity looks expensive because it is visible. Waiting costs are often distributed across customers, employees, lost sales, late projects, and risk. They can be less visible but much larger.

This perspective also explains why resilience and efficiency can conflict. A system designed for the average day may be efficient in calm conditions but fragile during peaks. A small capacity buffer creates an option to respond to unexpected demand without immediate restructuring.

The broader lesson is that idle capacity is not automatically waste. In a variable system, some slack is what allows work to flow. High utilization can be appropriate, but pushing every resource toward 100 percent can convert small fluctuations into long queues. Good operations management therefore asks not only, ‘How busy are our resources?’ but also, ‘How quickly does work move through the system, and how much variability must we absorb?’

Priority rules can further change queue performance. If every task is treated identically, urgent work may wait behind low-value work. A priority queue can improve response time for critical cases, but it may increase delays for lower-priority work and can create starvation if priorities are poorly designed. The policy should therefore reflect service commitments, not just convenience.

Little's Law provides another useful perspective: average work in process is related to throughput and average time in the system. Managers do not need advanced mathematics to use the insight. If throughput is roughly stable but the amount of work in process rises, cycle time will usually rise as well. Large piles of unfinished work are therefore not free inventory; they represent future waiting.

This matters in knowledge work because queues are often invisible. A factory can see physical inventory, but a consulting team may have dozens of open analyses, review requests, and decisions sitting in inboxes. Each unfinished item consumes attention and creates coordination cost. Reducing work in process can improve flow even without increasing individual productivity.

Simulation can help when the system is complex. Instead of relying only on average demand and average service time, teams can model realistic variation and test staffing levels, priority rules, or appointment policies. The goal is not perfect prediction but understanding how sensitive waiting time is to utilization and variability.
paragraphs.zh:
組織常追求高 utilization：客服希望人員都在接電話，工廠希望機器一直運轉，醫院希望昂貴設備充分使用，雲端團隊希望伺服器高效率負載。低 utilization 看似浪費，但系統一旦接近100%，等待時間往往會快速上升。

原因來自 queueing。工作抵達時間與處理時間都不是完全固定。即使平均 capacity 稍高於平均 demand，隨機波動仍會造成某些時刻需求超過即時處理能力。

有 spare capacity 時，忙碌過後 queue 可以縮回去；utilization 很高時，幾乎沒有多餘 capacity 吸收波動，新工作只能排在既有工作後面。

例如團隊平均每天能處理100件，收到90件時 utilization 90%，還有10件回復空間；若需求升到99件，看起來只多9個百分點，但 recovery capacity 從10降到1。小小 shock 就可能產生好幾天才能清掉的 queue。

因此 utilization 接近上限時，waiting time 通常是 non-linear 增加。

這對 staffing 很重要。主管看到員工偶爾 idle，可能想減人；但那些 idle period 其實可能是吸收需求波動的 buffer。把它拿掉，customer waiting time、abandonment、overtime 與 employee stress 都可能大幅上升。

Project team 也一樣。如果每位 specialist 都排到100%，任何突發問題都會讓下游 task 等待，開始 multitasking、頻繁換 priority、增加 coordination overhead。

Growing queue 不一定代表 demand 增加或員工不努力，也可能只是 variable arrival 和 service time 下，capacity 太接近極限的數學結果。

改善方法包括增加 capacity、降低 variability、把 simple/complex case 分流、標準化常見工作、用 appointment 或 pricing 把 demand 移開 peak period。Pooling 也有幫助。

不同 service requirement 需要不同 utilization target。可隔夜處理的 batch system 可以承受很高 utilization；需要立即 response 的 emergency service 必須保留更多 reserve capacity。

Measurement 應同時看 utilization、queue length、waiting time、abandonment、throughput 與 variability。

真正的經濟 trade-off 是 spare capacity 的成本與 waiting 的成本。Spare capacity 很顯眼，所以容易被當成浪費；等待成本卻散落在客戶、員工、lost sales、late project 和 risk 上。

Priority rule 也會改變 queue performance。Urgent work 可先處理，但 lower-priority work 會等更久，設計不良還可能 starvation。

Little's Law 提供另一個直覺：在 throughput 大致固定時，work in process 越多，平均 cycle time 通常也越長。知識工作裡 queue 常看不見，例如未完成分析、review request、待決策事項都堆在 inbox。

Simulation 可以用 realistic variation 測 staffing、priority、appointment policy。目的不是完美預測，而是理解等待時間對 utilization 和 variability 有多敏感。

因此 idle capacity 不一定是浪費。在有波動的 system 中，適度 slack 正是讓工作流動的條件。好的 operations management 不只問資源有多忙，也問工作流過系統有多快，以及需要吸收多少 variability。
paragraphs.ja:
組織はutilizationを最大化しがちです。call centerはagent、factoryはmachine、cloud teamはserverをできるだけ忙しくしたいと考えます。しかし100%に近いutilizationではwaiting timeが急増しやすくなります。

理由はqueueingです。work arrivalもservice timeも完全には一定ではありません。average capacityがaverage demandを少し上回っていても、random variationで一時的に処理能力を超えます。

spare capacityがあればbusy period後にqueueを縮められます。utilizationが高すぎるとvariationを吸収する余地がなく、新しいworkが待ち続けbacklogが増えます。

1日100 cases処理できるteamへ90件来るなら10件分のrecovery capacityがあります。99件になると余力は10から1へ落ち、小さなshockでもqueue解消に何日もかかります。

waiting timeはcapacity limitへ近づくほどnonlinearに増えることが多いです。

staffingでも重要です。idle minuteをwasteと見てheadcountを減らすと、そのidleがvariation吸収bufferだった場合、customer wait、abandonment、overtime、stressが増えます。

project teamも同じです。specialist全員を100% scheduleするとunexpected issueでdownstream taskが待ち、multitaskingやpriority change、coordination overheadが増えます。

growing queueはdemand growthやpoor effortだけでなく、capacityに近づきすぎた結果でもあります。

改善策にはcapacity追加、variation削減、simple/complex case分離、standardization、appointmentやpricingによるdemand shapingがあります。poolingも有効な場合があります。

service requirementによって適切なutilizationは違います。overnight batchは高utilizationでもよい一方、emergency serviceは大きなreserve capacityが必要です。

measurementではutilization、queue length、waiting time、abandonment、throughput、variabilityを一緒に見ます。

経済的trade-offはspare capacity costとwaiting costです。waiting costはcustomer、employee、lost sales、late project、riskへ分散し見えにくいです。

priority queueはcritical caseのresponseを改善できますが、low-priority workのdelayやstarvationを生む可能性があります。

Little's Lawの直感ではthroughputが安定している時、work in processが増えるとcycle timeも長くなります。knowledge workではopen analysis、review request、decision待ちがinboxに積み上がります。

simulationでrealistic variationを使い、staffingやpriority policyを試すこともできます。

idle capacityは必ずしもwasteではありません。variable systemでは一定のslackがwork flowを維持します。managementはresourceのbusyさだけでなく、workがsystemをどれだけ速く通過するかを見る必要があります。

quiz.question: Why can waiting time rise quickly near 100% utilization?
quiz.answer: There is too little spare capacity to absorb random variation.

quiz.question: Why can idle capacity have economic value?
quiz.answer: It provides recovery capacity and resilience during demand spikes.

quiz.question: Output: Name one way to reduce queueing delay without adding capacity.
quiz.answer: Example: reduce variability or shape demand.
